questions.prompt: Match each reporting job to the primary Oracle Fusion tool built for it, per lesson 1's four-job table.
left: Formatted financial statements that must look the same every period
Ad hoc, real-time exploration with no SQL required
Pixel-perfect, often scheduled output like a government form
Excel-native multidimensional analysis plus collaborative narrative packages
questions.explain: Lesson 1 maps each of the four reporting jobs to the tool purpose-built for it: Financial Reporting Studio for consistent formatted statements off GL balances, OTBI for ad hoc exploration, BI Publisher for pixel-perfect scheduled output, and Smart View for Excel-native analysis plus Report Packages. None of the four replaces the others.

questions.prompt: A client says: 'We need the 1099-MISC forms generated and emailed to each vendor automatically every January, in the exact required layout.' Which tool is the right fit, and why?
options: BI Publisher, because this needs a precise required layout delivered on an unattended schedule
OTBI, because it can export the current result of an analysis to PDF for distribution
Financial Reporting Studio, because tax forms are built against the GL balances cube
Smart View, because Report Packages support an author/review/sign-off workflow for regulatory filings
questions.explain: This request has two defining features from the Chapter 1 decision framework: an exact required layout (a government form) and unattended, automatic delivery on a recurring schedule. Both point squarely at BI Publisher, scheduled through the Scheduled Processes work area.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about function security and data security in Oracle Fusion reporting, per lesson 4.
options: Function security determines which reporting tools and subject areas a user can even open
Data security determines which rows of data a user sees once they're inside a tool they already have access to
A user with function access to OTBI automatically has unrestricted data access across every ledger
OTBI, BI Publisher, Financial Reporting Studio, and Smart View each enforce their own separate, independent security rules
Two users running the identical OTBI analysis can legitimately see different result sets, because of data security, not because the analysis is broken
questions.explain: Function security (duty roles) gates which tools and subject areas even appear for a user; data security (data access sets) then filters the rows returned once they're inside. The two layers are independent of each other, which is exactly why two users can run the same analysis and legitimately see different results. All four reporting tools share this one security model rather than inventing separate rules of their own, and function access never implies unrestricted data access.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the most common data-security mechanism in Fusion Financials is the ________, assigned to a user, which determines which ledgers (and segment values within them) that user can see balances for.
questions.explain: A data access set is the mechanism that scopes which ledgers, and which segment values within a ledger, a given user's reports and analyses can actually return data for — independent of whether that user has function access to the tool itself.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building a simple Financial Reporting Studio report in the order lesson 9 walks through them.
items: Start a new report and add a grid
questions.explain: Lesson 9's build sequence starts with the grid itself, then rows (what you're reporting on), then columns (what's being compared), then the point of view (which slice of the cube), then formatting, and finally a preview-and-save step before the separate publish step makes the report visible in the Financial Reporting Center.

questions.prompt: A Financial Reporting Studio report's title is typed as literal text reading 'Income Statement — March 2026' instead of referencing the point-of-view value. The point of view is then changed to April and the report is rerun. What happens?
options: The numbers update to April's balances, but the title still reads 'March 2026' because it was hard-coded instead of referencing the point of view
The report refuses to run until the title text is manually updated to match the new period
The title automatically updates to April, because every Financial Reporting Studio title is tied to the point of view by default
The numbers stay frozen on March's balances, because changing the point of view only affects the title, not the row and column data
questions.explain: Lesson 9 warns specifically about this habit: a title that references the point-of-view value updates automatically when the point of view changes, but a title typed as literal text does not. Rerunning the report pulls April's real numbers into the same rows and columns, while a hard-coded title just sits there unchanged, creating exactly the embarrassing mismatch the lesson calls out.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Account Groups are a reporting feature scoped to ________ only — they cannot be used to monitor open Payables invoices or Receivables transactions directly.
questions.explain: Account Groups are built from GL accounts and balances only. A request to watch open AP invoices or AR transactions needs a different tool — an OTBI analysis — rather than an Account Group.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Account Groups, per lesson 7.
options: An Account Group is a curated, flat list of chosen accounts, not a formal row-and-column statement
Account Groups are displayed in the Financial Reporting Center using the Sunburst radial visualization
Account Groups require defining formulas and a point of view the same way a Financial Reporting Studio statement does
Account Groups can be used to monitor both GL accounts and open Payables invoices at the same time
Account Groups are meant for casual, personal monitoring rather than a formal exhibit handed to an auditor
questions.explain: An Account Group is a flat, curated watchlist — pick the accounts, done — displayed with the Sunburst visualization, meant for casual monitoring rather than a formal exhibit. It deliberately skips the formula and point-of-view design work a full statement requires, and it's scoped to General Ledger only, so it cannot also monitor Payables invoices.

questions.prompt: A seeded Financial Reporting Studio report returns balances much lower than a controller expects for the period. Per lesson 6's troubleshooting order, what should be checked first, before assuming the report design itself is broken?
options: Whether the point of view (ledger, period, scenario) was actually set to what the controller intended
Whether the row and column formulas in the report design need to be rebuilt
Whether the GL balances cube needs to be deleted and recreated
Whether the controller's Smart View add-in is installed correctly
questions.explain: Lesson 6 lays out a specific order: check the point of view first (a report run against the wrong period or ledger will look wrong while actually being correct for the slice it was given), then data security, and only then the report design itself. Jumping straight to rebuilding the report is the common, avoidable mistake the lesson warns against.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inside an OTBI subject area, ________ are the measures you total or calculate — amounts, counts, quantities — while dimensions are the business attributes you slice them by.
questions.explain: A subject area organizes two kinds of things: facts, the measures to total or calculate (invoice amount, days overdue, transaction count), and dimensions, the attributes to slice those facts by (business unit, customer, supplier, period).

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about filters versus prompts in OTBI, per lesson 12.
options: A filter is a fixed condition set when the analysis is built, applying the same way every time it runs
A prompt lets the person running the analysis supply a value, such as a business unit, before the results render
A prompt is the right choice for a condition that should never change, like 'Payment Status = Unpaid' on an open-invoices analysis
A prompt can be given a sensible default value while still letting most viewers override it occasionally
Filters and prompts always produce identical results, because they both narrow the same underlying data
questions.explain: A filter is baked into the analysis permanently; a prompt lets each viewer, or each run, supply a different value, optionally with a sensible default. A condition that should never change, like restricting to unpaid invoices, is exactly the case for a fixed filter, not a prompt — the two are not interchangeable, since a prompt that always returns the same thing defeats its own purpose.

questions.prompt: A dashboard has three analyses on one page, and every one of them should always be sliced by the same Business Unit selection, without the viewer setting it three separate times. What's the right feature to use?
options: A dashboard-level prompt, applied once at the top of the page
A separate prompt added individually to each of the three analyses
A fixed filter hard-coded into each analysis for one specific business unit
Embedding each analysis separately inside the Payables work area
questions.explain: A dashboard-level prompt applies to every analysis on the page at once, which is exactly the right fit when multiple analyses on the same page should always be sliced the same way — far better than making the viewer set the same value three separate times, or hard-coding one business unit so nobody else can use the dashboard.

questions.prompt: Match each OTBI view type to what it's best suited for, per lesson 12.
right: A quick visual read of a trend or a share of total, rather than exact figures
Plain rows closest to a raw export, good for detail-level review
Rearranging dimensions across rows and columns with aggregated subtotals
questions.explain: Table is closest to a raw, row-by-row export, best for detail-level review. Pivot Table lets dimensions be rearranged across rows and columns with facts aggregated and subtotaled. Graph trades exact figures for a fast visual read of a trend or a share of the total.

questions.prompt: An OTBI analysis against the Payables Invoices subject area shows an invoice that was entered thirty seconds ago. A Financial Reporting Studio report run at the same moment does not reflect that invoice yet. Why?
options: OTBI queries live transactional data directly, while Financial Reporting Studio reports off a pre-summarized GL balances cube that's only as current as its last refresh
OTBI has a faster network connection to the Fusion database than Financial Reporting Studio does
Financial Reporting Studio is missing a duty role that OTBI has, so it can't see new transactions
The invoice was entered into a different ledger than the one Financial Reporting Studio is pointed at
questions.explain: This is an architectural difference, not a security or network issue: OTBI integrates with ADF to query live transactional data directly, while Financial Reporting Studio is built against a pre-summarized GL balances cube that only reflects data as of its last refresh. That's exactly why OTBI can show a thirty-second-old invoice that a cube-based report cannot yet.

questions.prompt: Match each BI Publisher term to what it actually is, per lessons 15-16.
right: A value a user supplies before the report runs, such as a date range, that flows into the query as a filter condition
The query, or queries, that return the rows and columns feeding the report
Defines how the retrieved data is laid out visually — fonts, tables, headers
Defines where the data comes from and what shape it's retrieved in, built from one or more data sets
questions.explain: A data model is the overall 'where does the data come from' definition, built from one or more data sets, each of which is an actual query. A template is the separate 'how does it look' layer. A parameter is a value the user supplies at run time that flows into a data set's query as a filter.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building an RTF template with the BI Publisher Template Builder in the correct order, per lesson 17.
items: Get sample XML from the data model
Build the Word document's visual layout
Insert fields and loops using the Template Builder add-in
Preview the template against the sample XML
Upload the finished RTF as the report's layout
questions.explain: A template author first gets sample XML to work against, lays out the visual design in Word, then uses the Template Builder add-in to map fields and loops onto that layout, previews the result against the sample data to catch problems early, and only then uploads the finished RTF to replace or supplement the report's layout in Fusion.

questions.prompt: A new template author builds an RTF invoice listing. At run time, the supplier name and invoice header print once for every single invoice line instead of once per invoice. What most likely went wrong?
options: The loop wrapping the repeating table row was drawn too wide, accidentally including the header fields inside the repeating loop instead of just the detail fields
The sample XML downloaded from the data model was corrupted
RTF templates can't support more than one field per page
The report was run against the wrong point of view
questions.explain: Lesson 17 calls out loop boundaries as the single most common source of malformed output for a new template author: if the loop meant to repeat only the detail row is drawn to also include the header fields, those header fields repeat once per detail row instead of once per invoice.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a BI Publisher report's recurring schedule is actually run by Oracle's ________, the underlying scheduling engine behind the Scheduled Processes work area.
questions.explain: The Enterprise Scheduler Service (ESS) is the engine that actually runs a scheduled job at its configured times, once a report has a job definition submitted through Scheduled Processes — nobody has to remember to click run.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about working with BI Publisher's predefined financial reports, per lesson 19.
options: Most real consultant work is running or lightly customizing an existing predefined report, not building a new data model from a blank page
When a predefined report is close but not quite right, the usual approach is copying its template and modifying the copy, rather than altering Oracle's original
Payables, Receivables, and Fixed Assets each ship their own sets of predefined reports suited to that module
A predefined report's template can never be modified under any circumstances
BI Publisher ships no predefined reports at all; every report must be built from scratch
questions.explain: Oracle ships a large catalog of predefined reports across financial modules, and a working consultant's job is far more often configuring or lightly customizing these than starting from a blank data model. When customization is needed, copying the template and modifying the copy preserves the ability to fall back to the seeded version.

questions.prompt: A user reports that Smart View won't connect to their Fusion environment. Per lesson 20's framing, what's the most likely category of problem to check first?
options: A data security or duty role issue — the same security model governing every other reporting tool — rather than a bug specific to Smart View
The version of Microsoft Excel installed on the user's machine, which must always be upgraded first
The GL balances cube, which must be rebuilt before Smart View can ever connect for anyone
The user's Payables invoice approval limits
questions.explain: Smart View relies on the exact same security model as every other tool in this course — no separate login, no separate rules. A connection failure is very often a data security or duty role issue rather than a Smart View-specific bug, which is exactly the troubleshooting instinct lesson 20 asks a consultant to build.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Report Package's development can include up to three phases — author, review, and ________.
questions.explain: Author, review, and sign-off are the three possible phases of a Report Package: contributors draft their sections, reviewers leave comments, and approvers formally sign off, creating a recorded trail before the package is published.

questions.prompt: Match each Smart View term to what it actually does, per lessons 21-22.
right: Re-queries the connected data source to pull current numbers into an existing worksheet layout
A structured, collaborative author/review/sign-off workflow for one shared deliverable
Rearranging which dimension sits on rows versus columns versus the fixed point of view
Navigating from a summary balance down into the detail that makes it up
questions.explain: Pivot rearranges dimensions between rows, columns, and point of view. Drill navigates from a summary balance into underlying detail. Refresh re-queries the connected source to update a worksheet's numbers while keeping its layout. A Report Package is the structured, multi-contributor author/review/sign-off workflow, a different kind of feature entirely from the single-user worksheet actions.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement comparing Smart View's distribution model to BI Publisher's, per lesson 23.
options: BI Publisher's model is built for unattended, recurring delivery with little judgment involved once it's scheduled
Smart View's distribution model assumes a human is actively building, reviewing, or refreshing the workbook
Smart View workbooks can be published to the Financial Reporting Center so others can open a live or recently refreshed version themselves
A static Excel export of a Smart View workbook stays current automatically after the next period closes
Report Packages are always PDF-based, so Smart View itself is never involved in reviewing one
questions.explain: BI Publisher's model is unattended and scheduled; Smart View's is built around active human involvement — building, reviewing, refreshing. A Smart View workbook can be published to the Financial Reporting Center for others to open a live version, but a static exported snapshot goes stale the moment the next period closes. Report Packages can be Word- or PowerPoint-based as well as PDF-based, and Smart View specifically handles reviewing the Word/PowerPoint kind.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the difference between the Income Statement and the Balance Sheet?
options: The Income Statement reports performance over a period of time, Revenue through Net Income; the Balance Sheet reports financial position at one point in time, where Assets equal Liabilities plus Equity.
The Income Statement reports financial position at a single point in time; the Balance Sheet reports performance over a period of time, Revenue through Net Income.
Both statements report performance over a period of time, differing only in which specific accounts each one happens to include.

The Balance Sheet is built by adding together a running total across every period since the company began, while the Income Statement always reports only a single period's ending balance in isolation.
The Income Statement and the Balance Sheet are simply two different names consultants use interchangeably for the exact same underlying report.
The Balance Sheet reports Net Income directly as its own line item, with no connection at all to Retained Earnings.
questions.explain: The Income Statement answers 'did this business make money during this period,' reporting performance from Revenue down to Net Income over a stretch of time. The Balance Sheet answers 'where do things stand right now,' a point-in-time snapshot where Assets equal Liabilities plus Equity. The two connect because Net Income flows into Retained Earnings on the Balance Sheet — they are related, not interchangeable or independent.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 2 is the closest wrong answer because it correctly recognizes that one statement is period-based and the other is point-in-time — it just assigns the two labels backwards. The Income Statement is the period-based one (performance over time); the Balance Sheet is the point-in-time one (position right now). Swapping which statement does which is exactly the mistake this lesson's framing is meant to prevent.

questions.prompt: A Balance Sheet's ending Retained Earnings this period does not equal last period's ending Retained Earnings plus this period's Net Income. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Something in the close process needs investigation — the two statements are never really independent, since Net Income flows into Retained Earnings every period
Nothing unusual — the Income Statement and the Balance Sheet are unrelated reports that commonly disagree with each other
The Balance Sheet should be rebuilt using a different account hierarchy specifically to hide the discrepancy
This is expected behavior whenever the point of view happens to span more than one ledger
questions.explain: Net Income flows into Retained Earnings period after period, so a Balance Sheet's ending Retained Earnings should always reconcile to last period's ending balance plus this period's Net Income. When it doesn't, that's a review point experienced consultants specifically check — a sign something in the close needs investigation, not something to paper over by rebuilding the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank to complete the accounting equation the Balance Sheet is structured around: Assets = Liabilities + ________.
questions.explain: The Balance Sheet's three sections — Assets, Liabilities, Equity — follow the accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity, with Equity including retained earnings accumulated from past periods' Net Income.

questions.prompt: Match each question a consultant might ask during close to the report that actually answers it, per lessons 25-26.
left: Does everything balance overall, for every account, this period?
Why does this one specific account have this balance?
What's overdue, bucketed by how many days past due?
What's the final, polished summary for someone outside accounting?
questions.explain: The Trial Balance is the GL's overall self-check that debits equal credits. Account Analysis drills into one account's full transaction detail when something looks off. The Payables Invoice Aging Report buckets unpaid invoices by how overdue they are. The Income Statement and Balance Sheet are the final, polished summaries meant for a reader outside accounting.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement comparing Payables aging to Receivables aging, per lessons 26-27.
options: Both bucket unpaid invoices into ranges like current, 1-30, 31-60, 61-90, and over 90 days
An aging Receivables balance is incoming cash that hasn't arrived yet, which directly affects how much cash the company has on hand
An aging Payables balance represents a company choosing, or being forced, to delay outgoing cash
Receivables aging feeds collections activity, prioritizing the oldest, largest past-due balances first
Payables aging and Receivables aging carry the exact same business urgency in every organization
questions.explain: Both aging reports use the same structure — current, then successive past-due buckets — but the business urgency runs in opposite directions: Receivables aging is cash not yet in the door, directly driving collections prioritization; Payables aging is cash the company is delaying (or being forced to delay) paying out. Treating the two as carrying identical urgency ignores exactly this distinction.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of building the month-end reporting package in the sensible order lesson 29 describes.
items: Confirm subledgers (Payables, Receivables, Fixed Assets, Cash Management) are closed
Run the Trial Balance and confirm debits equal credits
Run reconciliations, such as Payables-to-Ledger and bank statement reconciliation
Run AP and AR aging for the overdue-balance picture
Run the Income Statement and Balance Sheet last
questions.explain: Pulling any report before its source subledger closes produces incomplete numbers, so subledgers close first. The Trial Balance comes next because there's no point building polished statements on numbers that might not even balance. Reconciliations confirm each subledger ties to the GL, aging reports give the overdue-balance picture, and the headline Income Statement and Balance Sheet run last, once every supporting check is already clean.

questions.prompt: A Trial Balance shows one GL account with a balance that looks wrong, and a consultant needs to see every transaction that posted to that specific account during the period. Which statement correctly identifies the right next report and why?
options: Account Analysis, because it takes a single account and shows every transaction or journal line that moved its balance during the period
Trial Balance, run again, because rerunning the exact same report eventually surfaces the underlying transactions behind it
Account Analysis, because it shows every account's balance side by side the same way a Trial Balance does
The Income Statement, because it already breaks revenue and expense accounts down to the individual transaction level
The Payables Invoice Aging Report, because it already lists every transaction posted to any account in the general ledger during the period, not just Payables accounts
Account Groups, because the Sunburst visualization drills down into individual journal lines automatically
questions.explain: Account Analysis is built for exactly this situation: it takes a single account (or a small set) and shows every transaction or journal line that moved its balance during the period — the detail a Trial Balance deliberately leaves out. A Trial Balance shows every account's balance side by side but never drills into one account's transactions, which is why rerunning it again, no matter how many times, never surfaces that detail.
questions.distractorExplain: Option 3 names the right report but gives the wrong reason — 'shows every account's balance side by side' is actually a description of the Trial Balance, not Account Analysis. Account Analysis deliberately goes the opposite direction: one account, full transaction-level detail, not a side-by-side view of every account. Getting the right tool for the wrong reason is exactly the partial understanding this question checks for.
